To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bisphosphoryl peptide substrate binds VHR in a manner consistent with a ping-pong mechanism, that the phosphotyrosyl residue of the substrate is oriented into a deep pocket, and that the phosphothreonyl residue is loosely tethered by a basic pocket.
the crystal structure of a human DSP in complex with a MAP kinase substrate provides the first glimpse into the mechanism of substrate recognition for the DSP family.

The structure of the VHR phosphatase bound to a peptide substrate containing both phosphorylated threonine and tyrosine residues reveals that the phosphothreonyl residue is bound in a shallow pocket while the phosphotyrosyl residue is bound more tightly in the phosphatase active site cleft.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and mechanistic basis for substrate recognition and specificity of the human VHR phosphatase.
the structural and functional characterization of the human VHR protein phosphatase and the development of VHR inhibitors.
understanding how protein phosphorylation regulates the activities of protein kinases and phosphatases, which in turn regulate a broad array of cellular processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is the first structural study of a bisphosorylated substrate bound to a dual-specificity phosphates.
VHR is a dual-specificity phosphotyrosine phosphatase with a strong preference for bisphosphorylation of -pTXp- substrates.
this structure is the most complete description of a substrate-enzyme complex for any of the DSPs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have solved the structure for the first time of the substrate-enzyme complex for the dual-specificity protein phosphatase (DSP) family of enzymes.
VHR is a bisphosphopeptide phosphatase, which prefers to dephosphorylate phosphotyrosine over phosphothreonines within a bisphospho substrate.

VHR is an enzyme that is capable of binding to bisphosphoryl peptides, and the phosphotyrosyl residue of the peptide is bound into the active site of the enzyme in a manner that is very similar to the phosphotyrosines of the MAP kinase activation loop.
The main takeaway from our work is that
VHR binds its bisphosphoryl substrate by a unique mechanism that is distinct from other members of the DSP family of phosphatases.
VHR displays a preference for dephos-phorylating phospho-Tyr residues over phospho-Thr residues within bisphospho-rylated protein substrates.
the phosphotyrosyl binding site in VHR is a unique and deep pocket that may be exploited by future structure-based drug design efforts to generate phosphatase inhibitors.
